ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The diagram shows a horizontal base line. One line slants upward from the lower left to the upper right and forms angle α with the horizontal base near the left. Another line slants downward from the upper left to the lower right and forms angle β with the horizontal base near the right. A steeper transversal line descends from upper left toward lower middle, crossing the downward-slanting line at the angle labeled γ and crossing the upward-slanting line at the angle labeled δ. Reasoning: Use directed angles measured counterclockwise from the positive horizontal. The upward-slanting line has direction α = 55°. The downward-slanting line makes β = 40° with the horizontal, so its up-left direction is 180° − 40° = 140°. The steep transversal is closer to vertical and makes γ = 35° with the downward-slanting line, so its direction is 140° − 35° = 105°. The acute angle between the steep transversal and the upward-slanting line is 105° − 55° = 50°. In the diagram, δ is the adjacent obtuse angle at that intersection, so δ = 180° − 50° = 130°.

method.method_draft: First describe the image: the two diagonals and the horizontal base form a large triangle below their crossing point, while the steep transversal cuts the two diagonals on the left, forming a smaller triangle with the diagonals. In the large triangle, the base angles are alpha = 55° and beta = 40°, so the apex angle between the two diagonals is 180° - 55° - 40° = 85°. At the same crossing of the two diagonals, the angle used inside the smaller left triangle is supplementary to that 85° angle, so it is 180° - 85° = 95°. In the smaller triangle, the angle at the upper intersection is gamma = 35°. Delta is drawn as the exterior angle at the lower intersection of the steep transversal and the rising diagonal, so by the exterior angle theorem delta equals the sum of the two remote interior angles: delta = 95° + 35° = 130°.
